title: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna
hook: a wedding invitation carries two names joined by an ampersand. some Rig Veda hymns are addressed to two gods at once, joined into one word
carry: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna

segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna reached the fourth voice: a singer asking Varuna what he did wrong. Fire, storm, dawn, order. Which of the four stayed with you? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

A wedding invitation arrives in the mail. Heavy card, gold edges, and in the middle two names joined by an ampersand. Priya and Daniel. Not Priya, and somewhere below, Daniel. The two names are set in one line, sharing one symbol, because the invitation is about the two of them together. Some old hymns work the same way. In the Rig Veda, a god is often praised alone, Agni in one hymn, Indra in the next. But some hymns call on two gods at once, and Sanskrit has a way of joining their names into one word, so the pair is addressed like a single guest. Today: the gods who come in pairs.
screen: `TWO NAMES, ONE AMPERSAND.` → `SOME HYMNS CALL TWO GODS AT ONCE.` → `THE GODS WHO COME IN PAIRS.`

segments.voice: Sanskrit grammar doesn't stop at one and many. It keeps a form just for a pair. And it lets two names fuse. Mitra and Varuna become Mitravaruna, one word, spoken in the form for two. Indra and Agni become Indragni. Neither name is lost. They're just said together. The Rig Veda has hymns to both pairs. Varuna you've met as the keeper of order. Mitra, as an everyday word, means friend, and in the hymns he stands beside Varuna. So the keeper of order isn't praised alone. He's praised next to a friend. Read that slowly: the order that holds the world, and friendship, named in one breath. Indra and Agni make a different pair: the storm that breaks the drought, and the fire on the household hearth. A hymn can ask them to come together, to the same offering, as if the two strengths need each other. And Ushas, the dawn, keeps company with Agni without any grammar at all. The fire is lit at daybreak. In the hymns, the two arrive together: the light in the sky and the flame on the ground. So the poets didn't only picture each god on a pedestal of their own. They also pictured the gods as companions, called in twos, sharing a seat. On an ordinary Tuesday, the picture is close at hand. Look at almost anything good you did this week, and there's an ampersand in it somewhere.
screen: `A GRAMMAR FOR TWO.` · `MITRA AND VARUNA: FRIEND AND ORDER.` · `INDRA AND AGNI: STORM AND HEARTH.` · `USHAS AND AGNI ARRIVE AT DAWN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your pairs. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Then bring to mind two people who are better together than apart. A couple, two friends, a parent and a child, two coworkers who carry each other. Hold their names side by side, joined, like Mitravaruna. Notice what each brings that the other doesn't. Then ask: who am I paired with? Let a name come, and rest with it. If you pray, you can hold that pair in prayer. The bell holds the time.
Hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, the paired hymns: Mitra and Varuna, Indra and Agni, fused into one word and praised together. Today's word.

Your line: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, when something goes well, find the ampersand. Name the second person who made it happen, and tell them. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Vedic chanters learn the Rig Veda's hymns from a teacher, including hymns addressed to paired deities such as Mitra and Varuna or Indra and Agni, whose names are joined in a single dual-number word.

fork.setup: you're a Vedic poet. you want to praise the keeper of cosmic order. who do you set beside him?
fork.reveal: the hymns pair Varuna with Mitra, fused as Mitravaruna. order is praised next to a friend.

original.note: Sanskrit, the dual form: Mitra and Varuna named together as one pair. Stress shown is approximate.

trapdoor: what you thought: each Vedic god gets a hymn of their own.
what it means: some hymns call two gods together, Mitra with Varuna, Indra with Agni, as one invited pair.
what a scholar hears: a dual compound (dvandva in the dual), mitrāvaruṇā, indrāgnī: grammar built so two can be addressed as one.
recall: stilling the movements of the mind
the year just walked and kept
